raw_evidence: AWS provides an official SDK: 'The AWS SDK for Rust contains one crate for each AWS service, as well as aws-config ... a crate implementing configuration loading such as credential providers,' with full developer-guide documentation and code examples.

Microsoft has released an official Azure SDK for Rust, but only reaching beta status recently, with 'The initial release includes libraries for essential components such as Identity, Key Vault (secrets and keys), Event Hubs, and Cosmos DB,' a narrower service surface than AWS's.

Google Cloud offers a mix of official-style generated client libraries (e.g., google-cloud-support-v2, credited to 'googleapis, ... cloud-sdk-rust-bot') and long-standing community SDKs such as gcloud-sdk, indicating GCP Rust coverage is present but less unified/mature than AWS's.

Rust has an official, actively used MongoDB driver: 'Rust has an official MongoDB driver with async support ... written in pure Rust using tokio runtime,' and 'This repository contains the officially supported MongoDB Rust driver, a client side library that can be used to interact with MongoDB deployments in Rust applications.'

Mature community-maintained drivers exist for the other major databases, e.g., redis-rs offering 'a full implementation of the Redis communication protocol' using tokio as the async runtime, alongside widely used Postgres/MySQL crates.

gRPC integration is mature via the tonic crate, which is documented as the standard choice for building distributed Rust services with gRPC and is directly supported by the official OpenTelemetry OTLP exporter's grpc-tonic transport.

OpenTelemetry has an official, actively maintained Rust implementation under the CNCF open-telemetry organization providing 'the OpenTelemetry API crate ... required to instrument libraries and applications,' an SDK crate, and an OTLP exporter crate supporting traces, metrics, and logs to standard backends.

rubric.definition: Breadth and reliability of working, maintained external integrations: (1) official/major cloud-provider SDKs (AWS, Azure, GCP), (2) database drivers for major SQL/NoSQL systems, (3) messaging/streaming and RPC integrations (Kafka, AMQP, gRPC), (4) observability/tracing standard (OpenTelemetry) support, (5) CI/CD platform native support. Same dimensions and evidence approach (official SDK repos/docs, CNCF project pages, well-known crate ecosystem surveys) applied identically to all 10 languages; this shard scores only Rust.

dimensions.name: Official cloud SDK coverage (AWS/Azure/GCP) completeness and maturity
Database driver breadth/quality (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, etc.)

metric.external_integration_coverage.score_rationale: Rust's external integration coverage is strong and broad-based (official AWS SDK with full per-service coverage, official MongoDB driver, mature Redis/Postgres/MySQL crates, mature gRPC via tonic, and an official CNCF OpenTelemetry implementation) but is held back of a top score by the comparative immaturity of its Azure SDK (beta, narrow service list) and its fragmented/partly-unofficial GCP story, plus known gaps in individual drivers (e.g., historically missing GridFS support in the MongoDB driver, transactions initially unsupported).

selection_and_route.retrieval_route: web_search against official SDK repos/docs, CNCF project repo, and independent technical surveys

raw_evidence: Rust organizes platform support into three tiers with Tier 1 ('guaranteed to work') defined by official binary releases plus automated testing gating every merge, and Tier 2 ('guaranteed to build') covering a much larger set of targets.

A 2018-era internals discussion recorded Tier 1 support for three OSes (Windows, macOS, Linux) on x86/x86_64 (7 targets), and separately noted Rust already had Tier 2 support for 77 different targets spanning 36 different ISAs and about 13 different kernels including bare metal, with multiple toolchains (GNU, Android, MUSL) for some kernels — and the tier system has grown substantially since.

Tier 3 adds hundreds of further targets (e.g., new embedded/RTOS ports such as NuttX AArch64/ARMv7-A targets landing via ordinary PRs) with minimal centralized approval required, and Tier 3 requires no CI guarantee but still ships in the compiler tree.

WebAssembly is a first-class, increasingly-promoted target family: wasm32-wasip2 reached Tier 2 platform support starting in Rust 1.82, following the earlier wasm32-wasip1 rename, alongside the long-standing browser-oriented wasm32-unknown-unknown target.

The official platform-support documentation explicitly notes it is not exhaustive: 'those aren't the only platforms Rust can compile to' beyond the ones with built-in target definitions and/or standard library support, some targets support only core or alloc rather than full std (used for the most constrained embedded/bare-metal cases).

rubric.conversion: Sum of dimension scores, 0-100, applied identically to all languages using each language's own official target/platform documentation.
rubric.definition: Breadth of officially-implemented target/platform coverage: desktop/server OS x architecture combinations with strong guarantees, mobile OS as first-class compile targets, WebAssembly (browser + WASI), embedded/bare-metal (no_std) support, and total count/diversity of supported target triples across all tiers. Same rubric and evidence sources (official platform-support docs, target-tier policy page, official blog announcements) apply to all 10 languages; this shard scores only Rust.

dimensions.name: Desktop/server OS coverage at highest guarantee level (Windows/macOS/Linux, x86+ARM64)
Mobile OS as compile targets (iOS, Android)
Server/exotic architecture breadth (RISC-V, PowerPC, MIPS, s390x, etc.)
Total breadth of supported target triples across tiers 1-3 relative to general-purpose-language norms

metric.implemented_platform_coverage.score_rationale: Rust ships Tier-1 (fully guaranteed) support for Windows/macOS/Linux across the dominant architectures, Tier-2 support for iOS, Android, WASI (wasm32-wasip2) and dozens of ARM/embedded/server variants, and hundreds of Tier-3 targets spanning bare-metal microcontrollers, RTOSes, and exotic ISAs — one of the broadest implemented-platform footprints of any general-purpose language, trailing only C/C++ (via LLVM/GCC backends) in raw breadth, hence a high but not maximal score.

selection_and_route.retrieval_route: web_search against official rustc book / Rust blog / historical internals RFC thread
